deep_dives.title: VALUE with BASE: structures versus internal tables
deep_dives.explanation:
In `DATA(itab2) = VALUE ty_itab( BASE itab ( comp99 = 3 ) )`, the inner parentheses define a new table line. BASE copies all lines of `itab`, then one extra line is appended with `comp99 = 3` and everything else initial. Existing rows are not changed. This is a row-append, not a column update.

For structures the semantics differ: `VALUE ty_line( BASE structure comp99 = 3 )` starts from the structure's content and overrides the named component. Without parentheses on a table, `VALUE ty_itab( BASE itab comp99 = 3 )` is a syntax error, since a table needs line specifications.

To set a component on every row there are two patterns from the thread. First, a FOR loop: `VALUE ty_itab( FOR <line> IN itab ( VALUE #( BASE <line> comp99 = 3 ) ) )`. Here BASE applies to a structure, so it overrides the field per row. Second, copy the table and modify it in place: `MODIFY itab2 FROM VALUE #( comp99 = 3 ) TRANSPORTING comp99 WHERE comp99 <> 3.`

The in-place MODIFY avoids building a second table in the constructor and states the intent directly. In reviews, ask whether BASE is applied to a table or to a line, and whether the parentheses mean 'new row'.

deep_dives.title: CDS join pruning and declared cardinality: what to test
deep_dives.explanation:
The post (abstract only) measured on 7.55 and 7.58 which joins HANA drops when a consumer reads one field, which it never drops, and how a wrong declared cardinality changes row counts. The excerpt gives no numbers, so use it as a test design, not as a source of facts.

A lab can be built from the abstract. Create a CDS view with a to-one join and a to-many join. Read one field from the first table in a consumer. Inspect the generated SQL or plan in ADT and see which joins remain. Then change the declared cardinality and compare row counts, since a wrong declaration can change results as well as plans.

The principle to teach is that pruning depends on the optimiser knowing the join cannot multiply or drop rows. Cardinality is a promise the developer makes. Check the full post for its actual findings before presenting any of them as fact.

deep_dives.title: Per-user authorisation for AI agents calling SAP APIs
deep_dives.explanation:
Two posts show the guardrails around MCP servers. The S/4HANA server is read-only, calls only released OData APIs, goes through Cloud Connector and a BTP destination, and checks an allow-list against the system's own service catalog.

The CAP/Integration Suite post takes a different route: the agent reaches an MCP server in Integration Suite authenticated by IAS, then a BTP destination with OAuth2JWTBearer calls the CAP service as the authenticated user. Policies assigned in IAS decide access: a Catalog call works, an Admin call fails until the 'Admin' policy is assigned, with about one minute of delay. The author notes the consumer client ID must be named in the destination, which limits the MCP server to one client ID.

The design question is where the user identity is carried and where it is lost. Both excerpts are truncated, so verify destination and token steps against the full posts and SAP Help before reuse.

post_drafts.title: VALUE BASE trap
post_drafts.text:
*ABAP trap: VALUE with BASE on a table*

`DATA(t2) = VALUE ty_itab( BASE itab ( comp99 = 3 ) ).`

Does this set comp99 = 3 on all rows? *No.*
It copies itab and *appends one new row*, other fields initial.

Without the parentheses on a table: syntax error. BASE without parentheses works for structures only.

Fixes:
1) `VALUE ty_itab( FOR <l> IN itab ( VALUE #( BASE <l> comp99 = 3 ) ) )`
2) copy, then `MODIFY t2 FROM VALUE #( comp99 = 3 ) TRANSPORTING comp99 WHERE comp99 <> 3.`

https://community.sap.com/t5/abap-forum/prone-to-errors-value-base-itab-comp99-3/m-p/14503692#M1356

interview_questions.question: What does DATA(t2) = VALUE ty_itab( BASE itab ( comp99 = 3 ) ) produce, and how would you set comp99 = 3 on every row?
interview_questions.answer: It copies all lines of itab into t2 and appends one new line with comp99 = 3 and all other components initial. Existing rows are not changed, because the parenthesised group is a new line specification. Without the parentheses, BASE on an internal table is a syntax error; BASE without parentheses is valid only for structures. To change every row, use a FOR expression: VALUE ty_itab( FOR <line> IN itab ( VALUE #( BASE <line> comp99 = 3 ) ) ). Here BASE is applied to a structure, so the component is overridden per row. Alternatively, copy the table and run MODIFY t2 FROM VALUE #( comp99 = 3 ) TRANSPORTING comp99 WHERE comp99 <> 3, which changes rows in place.

interview_questions.question: A CDS view has several joins and a consumer reads one field. How would you check whether HANA prunes the unused joins, and what role does declared cardinality play?
interview_questions.answer: I would build a test consumer that selects only one field, then inspect the generated SQL and the execution plan in ADT to see which joins remain. I would do this for a to-one and a to-many join separately. Pruning is only safe if the optimiser knows the join cannot add or remove rows, so cardinality is a promise the developer makes. If the declared cardinality is wrong, row counts can change, so the result is wrong as well as the plan. I would test with the declared cardinality changed and compare row counts against the real data. I would measure on the target release rather than assume, since the CDS post reports results on 7.55 and 7.58 and I would want to confirm them.

interview_questions.question: Mass approval of 20 work items runs through an OData $batch changeset that calls a function module which commits workflow decisions. Where does the LUW boundary sit, and how would you handle item 14 failing?
interview_questions.answer: A changeset gives all-or-nothing semantics at the request level only if everything in it can be rolled back. A function module that commits internally ends the database LUW, so earlier decisions are already persisted when item 14 fails, and the changeset rollback cannot undo them. I would first check whether the decision API commits or can be called in update-task or without commit. If it commits, I would not claim atomicity. Instead I would process items individually, return per-item success or failure in the batch response, and define compensation for the already-decided items, such as a reversal action. If atomicity is required, the decision logic must be wrapped so that a single commit happens at the end of the changeset. The source post only introduces this problem, so the actual handling there is unverified.
